subject: Economics
description: Exports/imports, balance of payments, trade deficit, forex reserves

options.option_text: Only goods exports and imports
All economic transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a period
Federal budget only
Household savings

questions.explanation: BoP = current account + capital account + errors & omissions + change in reserves (balancing item). Current account = goods + services + income + transfers. Capital account = FDI, FPI, loans, remittances. BoP must always balance (double-entry).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: A country's TRADE DEFICIT occurs when:

options.option_text: Imports > Exports of goods & services
Exports > Imports
Exports = Imports
Foreign direct investment is high

questions.explanation: Trade deficit — value of imports exceeds exports. India has a persistent trade deficit (~$100-250 bn annually) due to high oil and gold imports. Partially offset by services-trade surplus (IT exports) and remittances. Different from fiscal deficit (government-spending).

questions.stem: India's FOREX reserves are managed by:

options.option_text: Finance Ministry
Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
SEBI
NITI Aayog

questions.explanation: RBI manages foreign exchange reserves. Current levels ~$600-700 billion (among world's top 5 by size). Composition: foreign currency assets (mostly US Treasuries), gold, SDRs (IMF), reserve tranche position. Crucial for managing rupee volatility, import cover.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Foreign Direct Investment
Foreign Debt Instrument
Federal Deposit Insurance
Financial Derivative Instrument

questions.explanation: FDI — foreign investor takes lasting interest (>=10% voting stake per IMF) in a domestic firm. Long-term, management-participating. FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment) — shorter-term, just buying shares/bonds. FDI in India managed via automatic / government approval routes across sectors.

questions.stem: India's LARGEST export category (historically and generally) is:

options.option_text: Agricultural products
Petroleum products + gems & jewellery + engineering goods
Tea
Handicrafts

questions.explanation: India's top export categories: engineering goods, petroleum products, gems & jewellery, organic chemicals, pharmaceuticals. In services, IT/software + business-process services dominate. Top import: crude oil / petroleum products, followed by gold, electronics.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Exports fall
Demand for its currency rises relative to other currencies
Forex reserves decline
Inflation accelerates

questions.explanation: Currency appreciates when demand for it > supply in forex markets. E.g., if dollar weakens (USD supply surplus / INR demand rise), rupee appreciates. Under floating rates, this happens naturally. RBI can intervene to smooth volatility by buying/selling dollars.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: A form of Indian currency
An IMF-created international reserve asset
Gold-backed certificates
Deposit insurance cover

questions.explanation: SDR — International Monetary Fund (IMF) unit of account, created 1969. Basket: USD, EUR, CNY (added 2016), JPY, GBP. Countries can use SDRs to buy hard currency from other member countries. India's quota reflects its share at the IMF. basket of 5 currencies.

questions.stem: In India's current account, which of the following is an example of an 'invisible export'?

options.option_text: Export of raw jute and jute products to Bangladesh markets
Forex earnings from software services exported to foreign clients
Export of iron ore and steel billets to Japan and South Korea
Sale of readymade garments and textile goods to US buyers

questions.explanation: Invisible exports are service receipts that earn foreign exchange without any physical good crossing the border — software services, tourism receipts, and transport earnings are classic examples. Options A, C, and D all involve physically shipped commodities, which are classified as 'visible exports' in the current account. India's IT/software sector is the largest contributor to invisible export earnings.

questions.stem: In which year did India formally accept the Article VIII obligations of the IMF, thereby achieving full current account convertibility of the rupee?

options.option_text: 1991, coinciding with the landmark structural adjustment programme
2000, when FEMA replaced FERA as the primary foreign exchange law
1994, when India fulfilled all conditions and accepted IMF Article VIII
1997, the year the Tarapore Committee submitted its roadmap report

questions.explanation: India formally accepted Article VIII of the IMF in August 1994, signifying that the rupee became freely convertible for all current account transactions (trade in goods and services). Option D is the most tempting distractor: the Tarapore Committee (1997) addressed capital account convertibility, a separate and still-incomplete step. Option B (2000) marks the legislative shift from FERA to FEMA, not convertibility acceptance.

questions.stem: Under the WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement, an importing country may levy anti-dumping duties when the foreign exporter's price is:

options.option_text: Below the 'normal value' — the domestic price or cost of production
Higher than prevailing international benchmark prices for the good
Equal to the landed cost including tariffs in the importing country
Agreed upon under bilateral preferential or free trade agreements

questions.explanation: Dumping occurs when an exporter prices goods abroad below their 'normal value', defined as either the home-market price in the exporting country or the full cost of production. GATT Article VI and the WTO Anti-Dumping Agreement authorise importing nations to impose duties equal to the dumping margin. Option B describes the opposite scenario. Option D (FTA pricing) is a legitimate arrangement and cannot be countered with anti-dumping duties.

questions.stem: A country's export price index rises from 120 to 140 while its import price index holds steady at 100. What has happened to its Terms of Trade?

options.option_text: Remained unchanged — ToT depends only on trade volumes, not prices
Deteriorated, as higher export prices are widely said to hurt competitiveness
Improved, since each unit of export now fetches more units of imports
Worsened, creating immediate pressure on the country's current account

questions.explanation: Terms of Trade = (Export Price Index ÷ Import Price Index) × 100. Here ToT = (140 ÷ 100) × 100 = 140, up from 120, so ToT has improved — the country gains more import purchasing power per export unit. Option B is a classic exam trap: higher export prices may reduce export volumes (a trade balance concern), but the ToT ratio itself still improves. Option A is wrong by definition — ToT is inherently a price-index ratio.

questions.stem: The term 'hot money' in international finance refers to capital flows that are:

options.option_text: Long-term and tied to greenfield manufacturing investments in host nations
Short-term, speculative, highly mobile across borders chasing rate differentials
Committed under bilateral investment treaties for infrastructure projects
Remitted by overseas workers to their home countries as family support

questions.explanation: Hot money describes highly liquid, short-term speculative capital — typically portfolio equity/debt flows or carry trades — that moves rapidly across borders in response to interest rate differentials or anticipated exchange rate movements. Unlike FDI (Options A and C), it can reverse overnight, amplifying exchange rate volatility. Option D describes worker remittances, which are current-account transfer inflows unrelated to speculative capital.

questions.stem: The Marshall-Lerner condition states that a currency depreciation will improve a country's trade balance only if:

options.option_text: The central bank simultaneously sterilises inflows by raising interest rates
The country's major trading partners are growing faster than the home economy
The depreciation is sustained for at least two consecutive quarters without reversal
The sum of absolute price elasticities of export and import demand exceeds unity

questions.explanation: The Marshall-Lerner condition (from Alfred Marshall and Abba Lerner) specifies: |PED of exports| + |PED of imports| > 1 for depreciation to yield a net improvement in the trade balance. If combined elasticity ≤ 1 (inelastic demand), the higher import bill outweighs any export revenue gain — this inelastic short-run phase explains the downward part of the J-curve. Options A–C describe monetary policy, partner-economy growth, and an arbitrary duration threshold, none of which are part of the Marshall-Lerner framework.

questions.stem: The 'J-curve effect' in trade theory predicts that a country's trade balance worsens immediately after currency depreciation before eventually improving. The primary cause of this initial deterioration is:

options.option_text: Exporters immediately raise foreign-currency prices to capture the full devaluation gain
The central bank sterilises reserve outflows by aggressively selling foreign currency
Trade contracts signed at pre-depreciation exchange rates take considerable time to renegotiate
Trading partners swiftly retaliate with countervailing duties on the depreciating country's exports

questions.explanation: The J-curve arises because, in the short run, trade volumes are sticky. Existing import and export contracts are denominated at old rates, so the local-currency cost of imports rises immediately while export volumes cannot surge overnight. As contracts expire and buyers respond to new price signals, export volumes expand and import substitution occurs — the trade balance improves, tracing a J-shape over time. Option A is incorrect: depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad, so exporters typically hold or cut foreign-currency prices to gain market share, not raise them. Option D describes a retaliatory trade-policy scenario, unrelated to the J-curve mechanism.
